conversation.content:
Hello there. I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is to support women as they adjust to new motherhood. I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that simply helps us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. Everything you share stays confidential between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you.

We’ll go through ten gentle questions. Most moms find it takes only a few minutes, and I’ll ask each one conversationally so you don’t have to remember any numbers or categories. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause. Ready to begin?

First question: Overall, in the past week, have you still been able to enjoy things the way you used to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[quiet breath, eyes on the blanket folded in my lap]  
I still like my coffee in the morning and the smell of the baby’s head, but… it feels muted? Like the volume got turned down. I’ll scroll pictures of him on my phone and know I should be beaming, yet it’s more of a tired smile than anything. Most things feel like I’m doing them because I’m supposed to, not because they spark anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh—like when my husband accidentally put the diapers on backwards—but it’s quick and then it’s gone. I’m not walking around chuckling the way I used to. Mostly it feels like I’m too tired or foggy to find things genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow shrug, rocking one foot]  
Not really. I mean, I tell myself I should be excited about little things—my mom’s coming next week, or we’re supposed to do a stroller walk with the neighbor—but it feels like one more task on the list. The “looking-forward” part barely shows up; it’s more like I’m bracing to get through it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes—like yesterday when he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking I must be missing some cue every other mom would catch. Or if he spits up a lot, I wonder if it’s because I ate the wrong thing. I know in my head it’s probably not my fault, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… a lot of the time. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel this tightness in my chest, picturing all these “what-ifs” about him—like what if he stops breathing in the crib, or what if I trip on the stairs while I’m holding him. Nothing specific sets it off; it’s just there, buzzing in the background.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full panic, but I’ll get these sudden waves—like I’m standing at the changing table and my heart starts racing and my stomach drops. It’s like my body thinks something awful is happening even though he’s right there, perfectly fine. It passes pretty quick, but it leaves me jittery.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s not one big thing—just the constant cycle of feed, burp, change, soothe, repeat. I’ll finally sit down and hear him stir, and it feels like the walls press in. I keep thinking, “I’m the adult, I should handle this,” but sometimes I just stare at the pile of laundry and feel like I’m drowning in tiny socks.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m lying there miserable… it’s more that my brain won’t shut off. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed, and then I’m running through did I sterilize the pump parts or whether his breathing sounded weird. I probably drop off around two, then I’m up again at four-thirty. So it’s not every night, but several.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do get hit with that sometimes—like yesterday evening when my husband asked how my day was and I just started tearing up over the casserole dish. It’s not a heavy cloud all day, but little waves of “ugh, this is hard” wash over me a few times a day, and I feel kind of… flat and weepy for a bit.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ll feel the tears build—like when he won’t latch or I spill the pumped milk—but I usually blink them back. Actual crying maybe once or twice this week, and it’s short, like a quick release, then I’m wiping my face and moving on.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I couldn’t leave him, and I’d never want to hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels muted-coffee and baby smells register faintly, events loom as chores, and waves of worry or sadness keep washing over you. Despite moments of laughter and deep love for your son, you describe feeling foggy, overwhelmed, and unable to look forward to things, all while blaming yourself whenever anything goes wrong.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing only in brief moments and feeling generally too exhausted or foggy to find things genuinely funny maps to 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost no anticipatory enjoyment, describing events as burdensome tasks rather than sources of pleasure, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent self-blame that intrudes despite rational awareness, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intrusive, and unprovoked worries occurring "a lot of the time" with physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Sudden waves of racing heart and stomach drops with no real danger map to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent daily overwhelm and inability to cope, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent (several nights) difficulty falling/staying asleep due to anxious racing thoughts, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, daily waves of sadness and tearfulness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 19 exceeds the 14-point cut-off for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorsed <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> (Q1-2, Q8), <sym>excessive guilt</sym> (Q3), <sym>daily anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic-like surges</sym> (Q4-5), <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym> (Q6), and <sym>sleep-onset difficulty</sym> (Q7). These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: ≥5 symptoms, same 2-week period, causing impairment. Absence of self-harm (Q10) lowers acute risk but does not rule out clinical depression. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss results and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and compatibility of <med>antidepressant medication</med> with breastfeeding
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress once treatment begins
4. Share these findings with your partner or a trusted support person so they can help you attend appointments and practice self-care
5. Prioritize rest by accepting help with overnight feeds, napping when baby sleeps, and light household duties
6. Engage in brief outdoor walks and gentle movement to boost mood and reduce <sym>anxiety</sym>
7. Contact local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or online communities to reduce isolation
8. If mood worsens or you ever feel unsafe, call 988 (US) or go to your nearest emergency department immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Mother, 3–4 wk post-delivery; Edinburgh responses embedded.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood / anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8)  
- Frequent tearfulness, “flat and weepy” episodes (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)  
- Intrusive, distressing anxiety (“what-ifs” about infant safety), occasional panic-like surges (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” difficulty completing daily tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty driven by ruminating worry (Q7)  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern  
Dysphoric mood coupled with marked anxiety and perceived inability to cope with routine infant care; symptoms present “several days” per week and interfere with functioning.

Screening significance  
- Meets provisional cut-off for probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety  
- No safety concerns voiced; protective factors (strong infant attachment, partner support) noted  
- Recommend formal EPDS scoring, clinical interview, and follow-up with OB/behavioral health for further assessment and possible evidence-based intervention (CBT, IPT, pharmacologic consult as indicated)
